query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coatings, the overall high‐temperature wear resistance is governed by the formation and mechanical integrity of an in‐situ developed protective oxide scale (comprising Cr2O3 and high-entropy spinel phases) that acts as a barrier against further oxidation and mechanical degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin film on a conventional steel substrate, with a typical, unmodified microstructure prior to any oxide scale formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal pre‐treatment (annealing in air at 800°C for 10 hours) to deliberately form a continuous, coherent oxide layer on the coating surface before wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regime ranging from 600°C to 900°C under sliding wear stresses (e.g., load of ~15 N and sliding speed around 2 m/s) in an air atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The thickness, continuity, and adhesion quality of the protective oxide layer (mainly Cr2O3 along with high-entropy spinel phases) that forms on the coating.
generation.mechanism: A coherent and adherent oxide scale can serve as a hard, low-friction barrier that both reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and mitigates further oxidation. This protective film, if mechanically stable under thermal cycling and load, prevents rapid degradation of the underlying coating, hence enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to as-deposited coatings, the thermally pre-treated coatings will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate and friction coefficient in high-temperature wear tests. Post-test microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/EDS) should reveal a more uniform, intact oxide scale that remains well-bonded to the coating-substrate interface.
generation.baseline: Untreated (as-deposited) FeNiCrCoCu thin film coatings without deliberate oxide layer formation.
generation.boundary: Valid for thin-film protective applications at temperatures between 600°C and 900°C, under moderate to high sliding loads (around 15 N), using steel as the substrate and testing in an atmospheric (air) environment.
generation.uncertainty: It is not fully established how the dynamics of oxide scale formation and potential fragmentation translate from studies on bulk or alternative HEA systems (e.g., evidence from PMC10908794::web::051 and PMC7241466::web::012) to the specific case of a FeNiCrCoCu thin film. Moreover, the optimal annealing protocol for achieving maximum oxide integrity over repeated thermal-mechanical cycles is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin film coatings on steel substrates: one as-deposited (baseline) and one pre-treated by annealing in air at 800°C for 10 hours. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., at 800°C under a 15 N load and 2 m/s sliding speed). Characterize the wear tracks and oxide layer morphology using SEM/EDS.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Oxide layer thickness, continuity, and adhesion quality via SEM/EDS
Post-test surface and interfacial damage assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the pre-treated coatings do not show a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower wear rate and friction coefficient) compared to the baseline or if microstructural analysis reveals that the oxide layer is fragmented or poorly adherent, resulting in no protective benefit under the tested high-temperature wear conditions.
